headline: The sudden reversal in the stock market, and what comes next
author: John Csiszar

paragraphs.text: If you haven’t looked at your investment accounts over the past two months or so, you might be in for an unpleasant surprise. As of early October, the S&P 500 was up more than 14 percent for the year. But after an 11.6 percent decline from its peak, those gains have nearly vanished. As of Friday’s close, the index was up less than 1 percent for 2026, excluding dividends. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite has turned negative, down 2.7 percent on the year.

The S&P 500, Dow and Nasdaq are all now in corrections, meaning they’ve fallen more than 10 percent from their recent highs. With the artificial intelligence-fueled stock boom petering out, many investors are concerned just what it means for the overall market and what they should do with their portfolios now.
Investors have poured money into AI-related stocks, while the companies themselves have spent billions of dollars on data centers, advanced computer chips and other infrastructure.

Recently, however, investors have begun questioning whether all that AI spending will generate enough profits to justify the lofty stock prices. Some of the same companies that helped push stocks higher earlier this year are now pulling the market down.
Corporate earnings, meanwhile, have remained strong. According to FactSet, S&P 500 companies are reporting third-quarter earnings growth of 32.9 percent compared with a year earlier.
The problem, according to Dustin Wigington, founder of wealth management firm Rulicent Investments, is that investors expected even more.

“The success of artificial intelligence as a technology and the success of AI stocks as investments are two entirely different things. A company can be enormously successful while its stock disappoints. The price you pay matters,” Wigington said.

Persistent inflation and the prospect of additional interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve have added to investors’ concerns. But even with all of these worries overhanging the market, Wigington cautioned against assuming the recent downturn will become a prolonged market decline.
In an interview, he pointed to the sharp sell-off in late 2018, when the S&P 500 fell nearly 20 percent from its September peak before rebounding strongly in 2019.

Wigington described the current downturn as a classic, healthy correction, although there’s no guarantee of a quick recovery. And some financial commentators have warned that the AI-driven boom in the stock market has set the stage for a much deeper bust, predictions the markets have defied for much of the past two years.

Investing can be emotional, especially when the markets are in turmoil. The key, many financial advisers say, is to avoid disrupting long-term investment plans while still paying attention to what’s going on.

“Staying the course is one of the most powerful things an investor can do. Market volatility is inevitable, and it’s not wise for investors to change their strategy in response to short-term market moves,” said Alex Michalka, vice president of investment research at Wealthfront, an automated investment management and financial planning firm.

Michalka recommends reviewing your portfolio at least annually to make sure it still matches your financial goals — both in terms of your investment objectives and risk tolerance. Making small adjustments in line with your original investment strategy is a better move than making wholesale changes based on the latest headlines, he said.

Check how you’re handling the market volatility as well. If the recent market turmoil makes you lose sleep at night, Michalka said, it’s possible that your asset allocation was riskier than appropriate for you personally.

Your timeline also plays an important role. Michalka said investors in their 60s and nearing retirement usually have different risk profiles than younger investors and should think carefully about how much risk they can tolerate, including how they’d handle another substantial decline.
Similarly, money needed for short-term expenses shouldn’t be exposed to the same stock market risks as long-term savings.

Corrections may be a normal part of investing, as Wigington pointed out. But that’s probably of little consolation to anyone who’s watched nearly a year’s worth of gains disappear in a matter of weeks. For those investors, the more pressing question is whether their portfolios are prepared for what comes next.
